title: The hidden side of providing feedback: knowing what emotions are triggered
author: Mueller, Kurt
source: The Hidden Side of Leadership, August 2, 2026
summary: Kurt Mueller's leadership newsletter highlights that people do not learn from feedback simply because they receive it—they learn when the emotional response that feedback triggers keeps attention focused on improving the work rather than defending the ego. Mueller reframes ambition as the desire to make a larger impact rather than to accumulate money or status, and shares curated insights on decision-making under uncertainty, advocating for one's own work, and leading through transitions.
points: Feedback only drives improvement when the emotions it triggers direct attention toward the work rather than self-protection; leaders must understand what emotional response their feedback produces.
Ambition is better defined as the desire to make a greater impact than as the desire for money, status, or fame—this reframing changes how leaders develop and support ambitious people.
Leaders must make their own work visible and understood: good execution that goes unseen or undervalued wastes organisational capacity and undermines influence.
Not all information deserves equal trust; distance from operational reality progressively weakens decision quality, and leaders must recognise and compensate for this.
Leadership transitions—including time between roles—should be approached as developmental opportunities rather than gaps; the discipline of leadership does not pause between jobs.
quotes: Now on to the key tools, tactics and ideas for your consideration: People don’t learn from feedback simply because they receive it—they learn when the emotions feedback triggers keep their attention focused on improving the work rather than protecting themselves.
Given this time of disruptions and uncertainty for most of my leadership practitioners I have had to take a closer look at transitions.
And there are a lot of ways to make an impact that have nothing to do with money, status, or fame.
Too often ambition is assumed to be about a desire for money, status, or fame.
The truth is simpler than that: Ambitious people want to make a bigger impact.
